q.intro.text: Two equations share the same x and the same y. x plus y equals seven, and x minus y equals one. Which marked point makes both of them true? Pick one, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one. The graph moves first, then the notation.

e.step0.text: Every pair that adds to seven is a solution: one and six, two and five, five and two, and more. They all sit on one line, the line of x plus y equals seven.

e.step1.text: The pairs whose difference is one sit on a second line, the line of x minus y equals one.

e.step2.text: The lines cross at four, three. It is the one point on both. Check: four plus three is seven, and four minus three is one. Both true. Five, two is on the first line only: five minus two is three, not one.

e.step3.text: Add the equations. The y's cancel: two x equals eight, so x equals four. That is the line x equals four, and it runs through the crossing. Then four plus y equals seven, so y equals three. The solution is four, three.

e.why.text: Quick check. Why is the crossing point the solution of the system?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. A point on a line makes that line's equation true. On both lines means both equations.

e.why.axis.text: Seven, zero is where the first line meets the x axis. But seven minus zero is seven, not one. It is on one line only.

e.why.one.text: Five, two is on the first line: five plus two is seven. But five minus two is three, not one. A solution has to fit both.

t.intro.text: Solve y equals two x minus one, and x plus y equals eight. The graph is done for you. The algebra is yours.

t.sub.text: Put the first equation into the second: y is replaced by two x minus one. Which equation do you get?

t.sub.ok.text: Yes. y is the whole two x minus one, so it goes in with its parentheses.

t.sub.first.text: y equals all of two x minus one, not just two x. Keep the minus one.

t.sub.wrong.text: The first equation tells what y is, so y is the letter you replace.

t.x.text: Solve three x minus one equals eight. What is x?

t.x.sign.text: Three x minus one equals eight. Add one on both sides, so three x equals nine.

t.x.nine.text: Nine is three x. One more step: divide by three.

t.x.no.text: Add one on both sides, then divide by three.

t.x.ok.text: Yes. Three x equals nine, so x equals three. That is the line x equals three, through the crossing.

t.pair.text: Now find y, and give the solution as a pair.

t.empty2.text: Type both numbers of the pair.

t.pair.rev.text: Right numbers, wrong order. x comes first in the pair.

t.pair.y.text: x equals three is right. Put it into y equals two x minus one to find y.

t.pair.no.text: x equals three. Put it into y equals two x minus one, then write the pair, x first.

t.pair.ok.text: Yes. y equals two times three, minus one, which is five. The solution is three, five, right where the lines cross.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked four, three, and you were right. It is the one point on both lines.

q.cb.one.text: At the start you picked five, two. It fits the first equation, but not the second. A solution has to fit both.

q.cb.rev.text: At the start you picked three, four. Those are the right numbers in the wrong order: x comes first.

q.cb.none.text: A solution of a system is the one pair that fits both equations: where the lines cross.

p.intro.text: Riley solves y equals two x plus three, and y equals two x minus one. Setting them equal, the x's cancel and leave three equals negative one. Riley writes x equals zero, so the solution is zero, three. Is Riley right?

p.test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.no.zero.text: The x's cancelling does not make x zero. It left three equals negative one, a false statement, whatever x is.

p.no.far.text: The gap between these lines is four everywhere. Draw them as far as you like: it never closes.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.c1.text: Right. Zero, three is on the first line only. At x equals zero, the second line is at negative one.

p.c2.text: Right. Same slope, different starting points. The gap between the lines is four everywhere.

p.c3.text: Right. Three equals negative one is false for every x, so no pair fits both. That is what parallel lines look like in algebra.

p.done.text: That's a proof: three claims, each with its reason, and the graph backs every one. When the letters cancel and leave a false statement, there is no solution.
